## Part I — Application Links & System Architecture

- **Interactive Shiny App URL:** <https://jordanblackman.shinyapps.io/ads506-retail-forecasting-app/>
- **Source Code Repository:** <https://github.com/jblackman-bit/ADS-506/tree/main/Module%205>

**Executive Summary:** This cloud-deployed Shiny dashboard provides an interactive forecasting platform analyzing 416 continuous months (1992–2026) of U.S. Census Bureau retail trade sales. Designed for supply chain leaders, the application contrasts real purchasing volume (CPI-adjusted) against nominal cash flows, dynamically fits competing predictive algorithms (TSLM, ETS, Seasonal ARIMA, Ensemble Combo), and decouples retrospective validation backtesting from forward operational projections.

**Core Application Features:**

- **Dynamic Tsibble Exploration:** Interactive vertical filtering, historical date range controls, and real (CPI-deflated) vs. nominal valuation toggle to isolate true consumer demand from monetary inflation.
- **Decoupled Analytical Engine:** Separates held-out historical validation backtesting (Model & Accuracy tab) from 6- to 36-month forward production forecasts (Comparative Forecasts tab).
- **Executive Diagnostics & Intervals:** Mathematical model orders, color-coded goodness-of-fit scorecards, and 80%/95% prediction intervals with actual history overlays.

## Part II — Executive Data Story

**Context: Structural Divergence Behind Macro Aggregates**\
Aggregated retail totals mask critical divergence across consumer sectors. While essential **Health & Personal Care** exhibits compounding, non-cyclical real growth (+180% since 1992), discretionary **Clothing & Accessories** volume has remained completely flat for 24 years despite massive December holiday surges. Building materials peaks in May--June aligned with residential construction cycles. Reliable supply chain planning requires models that accommodate these contrasting seasonal and cyclical dynamics.

### Strategic Conflict: Why Does Linear Regression (TSLM) Fail?

When evaluating out-of-sample forecast accuracy over a 12-month validation horizon, **Time Series Linear Models (TSLM)** perform drastically worse than modern dynamic algorithms across every retail vertical, generating **2.1**$\times$ to 4.6$\times$ higher forecast errors (e.g., Macro RMSE of \$9,108M for TSLM vs. \$1,975M for ETS). This severe failure stems from three fundamental mathematical limitations:

1.  **Rigid Deterministic Trend:** TSLM enforces a static, straight-line slope ($\beta_1 t$). It cannot adapt to structural economic inflections, recessions (2001, 2008, 2020), or compounding curves (Health exponential expansion vs. Apparel stagnation), leading to massive multi-billion-dollar baseline drift.
2.  **Static Additive Seasonality:** TSLM fits constant seasonal dummy coefficients ($\sum \gamma_j D_j$), forcing identical dollar swings each year. Because real retail demand is *multiplicative*, holiday surges expand in dollar scale as total revenue grows; TSLM severely underestimates Q4 peaks and distorts troughs.
3.  **Zero Dynamic Memory (White Noise Error Assumption):** Ordinary least squares assumes independent errors ($\varepsilon_t \sim i.i.d.$), ignoring serial correlation, inventory momentum, and multi-month supply shocks. Unlike ARIMA and ETS, TSLM cannot self-correct after an initial forecast error.

**Remedying Linear Regression in Practice:**\
To salvage regression for retail operations, planners must: (a) employ **Dynamic Regression (ARMAX)** incorporating macroeconomic regressors such as **CPI (inflation deflator)**, disposable income, and consumer sentiment into the error structure; (b) incorporate **calendar/trading-day regressors** (counting peak shopping Saturdays and days between Thanksgiving and Christmas); and (c) apply **logarithmic transformations** ($\log Y_t$) or spline trends to model multiplicative seasonal growth and cyclical bending.

\vspace{-4pt}

**Resolution & Implementation:** Operational planners must abandon rigid OLS models for inventory commitments. Supply chains should deploy $\text{ETS}(M,A,M)$ for apparel holiday planning and Seasonal ARIMA for housing materials, preventing costly stockouts while maintaining lean working capital.\
